value.overview: The Snowy Plover is a small, pale shorebird of open beaches, mudflats, salt ponds, and other sparsely vegetated coastal habitats. It has a compact body, short dark bill, dark legs, and distinctive dark patches on the forehead, behind the eye, and on the sides of the neck in breeding adults. Its sandy-brown plumage provides excellent camouflage. The species occurs across much of the Americas, with separate coastal and inland populations.
value.classification: The Snowy Plover belongs to the plover family Charadriidae and the order Charadriiformes. Its current scientific name is Anarhynchus nivosus; it was formerly widely known as Charadrius nivosus.
value.identification: This is a small, short-legged plover with a rounded head, short thin bill, dark eyes, and dark legs. Adults are grayish brown above and white below. Breeding birds show black marks on the forehead, around the eyes, and on the sides of the neck; these markings become reduced or brownish in nonbreeding plumage and young birds. It is generally paler and smaller-looking than many other beach plovers. Its quick running, frequent stops, and low feeding posture are characteristic.
value.rangeHabitat: The Snowy Plover occupies coastal shores and inland saline environments from western and central North America through parts of Central and South America and the Caribbean. It favors wide sandy beaches, dry upper beach, sandflats, coastal lagoons, salt pans, mudflats, and alkaline lake margins with little vegetation. In Costa Rica it is a migrant, mainly encountered along suitable Pacific and Caribbean coastal habitats and associated wetlands rather than as a regular breeding resident. Records are local and seasonal, and it may be overlooked because of its camouflage.
value.migrationStatus: The species includes both resident and migratory populations. In Costa Rica it is generally treated as a migrant or seasonal visitor, with individuals arriving from breeding areas farther north and using coastal habitats and wetlands during the nonbreeding period. It is not considered a regular resident breeder in the country.
value.breeding: Snowy Plovers usually nest on the ground in open, sparsely vegetated sites, often on upper beaches, sandflats, salt ponds, or dry lake margins. The nest is a shallow scrape, sometimes lined with small shells, pebbles, or plant fragments. Both adults may participate in territorial defense, while males commonly perform courtship displays and prepare scrapes. Clutches typically contain three eggs, and the precocial chicks leave the nest soon after hatching. Nesting success is strongly affected by disturbance, flooding, predators, and vegetation encroachment.
value.dietFeeding: Snowy Plovers feed mainly on small invertebrates, including insects, insect larvae, crustaceans, marine worms, and other shoreline prey. They forage visually by running a short distance, stopping, and making rapid pecks at prey on the surface or in shallow sediment. They may also probe wet sand, wrack, mudflats, and the edges of shallow pools. Feeding activity is often concentrated around tidal changes or during periods when prey is exposed.
value.behavior: This plover is usually active on foot and spends much of its time moving quickly across open ground while foraging. It often crouches or freezes when approached, relying on camouflage, and may give soft calls while traveling or defending a feeding area. Snowy Plovers can gather in loose flocks outside the breeding season, sometimes with other small shorebirds. When disturbed, they commonly run before taking flight and may circle low over the beach.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, although trends vary among regions. Local management has improved numbers in some protected areas, but many coastal populations remain vulnerable and fragmented.
conservation.threats: Major threats include loss and degradation of beaches, salt flats, lagoons, and other open nesting areas; coastal development; intensive recreation; vehicles, dogs, and beach grooming; disturbance of nests and chicks; introduced vegetation that changes open habitat; predation; pollution and oil spills; flooding; and rising sea levels. In Costa Rica, disturbance and habitat alteration at coastal wetlands and beaches may reduce the quality of stopover and wintering sites.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect undeveloped beaches, salt ponds, coastal lagoons, and other open shorebird habitats. Keep dogs leashed where shorebirds occur, avoid driving on beaches, stay outside marked nesting or roosting areas, and do not approach flocks closely. Support protected-area management, habitat restoration, responsible coastal development, and shorebird monitoring. Reporting well-documented observations through recognized bird-monitoring programs can help clarify seasonal distribution in Costa Rica.
